Well, happier? I don't know if "happier" is the right word. I mean, happiness is subjective, isn't it? For me, it's not really about walking around with a smile on my face because I dropped a pound or two. It's more about... well, it's about satisfaction, I guess. I look in the mirror, and if I see any softness, any sign that I'm slipping into that complacent, middle-aged stereotype, it just eats at me. Maintaining the standard I set for myself thirty years ago. I don't think that's about happiness, exactly, just... not letting myself fail.

Afraid? I mean... I wouldn't use the word afraid, exactly. Fear is what you feel when you're clearing a dark building and you don't know who's behind the door. But... if you're asking if it bothers me, if it gets under my skin? Yeah. Yeah, it does. It's more of a... a visceral reaction. 

Let me explain it like this. Every morning, right after I wake up, before I even have a sip of water, I step on the scale. It's just part of the routine, right? Like shaving or putting on the uniform. But if that number is up—even by a fraction, even just half a pound—it's like... it's like a physical jolt. It hits me right in the chest. It's this immediate sense of failure, this overwhelming feeling that I've completely lost control. I start running through everything I did the day before, every single thing I put in my mouth, trying to figure out where I slipped up. And the rest of the day? It's ruined. I can't focus on anything else. I'll spend the entire shift just... obsessing over it, making sure I cut back even harder. No coffee with milk, no yogurt, nothing. Just water. Because the idea of putting weight back on, of letting that number creep up and up until I'm just another out-of-shape cop... I can't stand it. It makes my skin crawl just thinking about it. I've worked too hard, for too many years, to let myself go like that. So, afraid? Maybe not afraid in the traditional sense. But I absolutely refuse to let it happen. I just can't.

========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Well, it's not like I have a specific number written down on a piece of paper, or a picture of some fitness model taped to my bathroom mirror. It's not about trying to look like someone else, or hitting some arbitrary metric that some doctor—no offense—decided was healthy. It's more about what I see when I look at myself. And the thing is, when I look in the mirror, I don't see what the occupational health guy sees, or what my sergeant sees when they tell me I'm looking gaunt. They use words like that—gaunt, frail. I don't see that at all. 

When I stand in front of that mirror, usually right after the scale, my eyes just zero in on my stomach and my waist. That's the battleground right there. If I can pinch anything, if there's any softness, any lack of definition around the beltline... it's just unacceptable. I'll stand there, turning side to side, checking the lines, checking the firmness. And honestly, I judge my whole day by what I see in those few minutes. If I look lean enough, if my stomach is flat and tight, then I feel like I can respect myself. I feel like I've earned the right to put on the uniform and go out there and do my job. But if I don't... if I see even a hint of slackness, it just ruins me. I feel disgusted. I feel like a fraud. It's like, how can I demand respect on the streets if I can't even maintain discipline over my own body? So, it's not a specific weight, exactly. It's a standard. A standard of looking lean enough that I don't feel ashamed of the man looking back at me.

Well, if I didn't have concerns about my weight... see, it's really hard to separate the two. It's all tied up in this whole idea of discipline I was just talking about. I mean, the whole reason I'm even sitting in this chair talking to you right now—what actually brought me in—is because the occupational health department at the precinct got involved. You don't want to be sluggish or weighed down when you're out on the street, especially not at my age. You need to be ready to move. So it's just the black coffee, and then... maybe, if I really feel like I need something, I'll have a plain yogurt. Then when I finally get home after a twelve-hour shift, I might have a few bites of chicken at night. Just enough protein to keep the engine running, so to speak. 

Occupational health thinks that's completely unreasonable, but if I were to sit down and eat a whole, regular, full meal... it just feels wrong. Even if I didn't care about the number on the scale or the softness around my waist, sitting down to a big plate of food just feels like I'm letting my standards slip. It feels like I'm giving in to comfort, like I'm throwing away all that mental toughness I've built up over thirty years on the force. The act of eating a full meal itself, of getting full and heavy, it just feels like complacency. Like I'm dropping my guard. And I've spent my entire career learning never to drop my guard, so... I just can't bring myself to sit down and eat like everyone else does. It's just not who I am anymore.

========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Well, that’s the million-dollar question, isn't it? Success. You see, being a police officer—especially when you've been on the force as long as I have, over thirty years now—it’s not just a job you clock in and out of. It’s an identity. When I first joined the academy back in the day, they drilled this concept into us called "command presence." You walk into a room, a domestic dispute, a chaotic scene on the street, and people need to know instantly that you are in charge, that you have authority, and that you are completely in control of the situation. 

And how do you project that control if you don't even have control over your own physical form? So, to answer your question... no. No, I really don't think I could consider myself a success if I weren't as lean as I am now. If I let myself go, even a fraction of an inch, I’d feel like a total failure. 

It goes back to exactly what I was trying to explain to you earlier about my morning routine. When I look in the mirror, I just don't see what everyone else says they see. The occupational health doctor, the young nurse, Sal down at the quartermaster—they look at me and see someone who is, what did they say, "dangerously low" or frail. But I look in that exact same mirror and my eyes just bypass all of that and focus entirely on my stomach and my waist. That is the ultimate measure of a man's discipline. 

I literally judge my whole day, my entire sense of worth, by whether I look lean enough right there at the beltline to respect myself. If I wake up and I look in that glass and I see a flat, hard, perfectly lean stomach, then I can put on the badge. I can go out there and be a cop. I have the right to enforce the law because I am enforcing the strictest laws on myself. But if I wasn't this lean? If I was soft? I wouldn't have any self-respect. And if I don't respect myself, the guys on the street sure as hell aren't going to respect me. I've seen guys on the force who let themselves get a gut, who sit in the cruiser eating junk all day, and they're a joke. I swore I would never, ever be that guy. So my success is entirely tied to keeping that edge, keeping that sharpness, no matter what anyone else thinks they see when they look at me.

It's like, how can I demand respect on the streets if I can't even maintain discipline over my own body? So, it's not a specific weight, exactly. It's a standard. A standard of looking lean enough that I don't feel ashamed of the man looking back at me.\n\nDoctor: Do you think you would still restrict your food intake if you didn't have concerns about your weight?\n\nPatient: Well, if I didn't have concerns about my weight... see, it's really hard to separate the two. Well, they kind of bleed into each other, don't they? But... if you're really forcing me to split hairs, to get right down to the brass tacks of it... I'd have to say it's the shape. I start running through everything I did the day before, every single thing I put in my mouth, trying to figure out where I slipped up. And the rest of the day? It's ruined. I can't focus on anything else. I'll spend the entire shift just... obsessing over it, making sure I cut back even harder. No coffee with milk, no yogurt, nothing. Just water. Because the idea of putting weight back on, of letting that number creep up and up until I'm just another out-of-shape cop... I can't stand it. It makes my skin crawl just thinking about it. I've worked too hard, for too many years, to let myself go like that. So, afraid? Maybe not afraid in the traditional sense. But I absolutely refuse to let it happen. I just can't.\n\nDoctor: Do you have a specific weight or body shape in mind that you're trying to achieve?\n\nPatient: Well, it's not like I have a specific number written down on a piece of paper, or a picture of some fitness model taped to my bathroom mirror. It's not about trying to look like someone else, or hitting some arbitrary metric that some doctor—no offense—decided was healthy. It's more about what I see when I look at myself. And the thing is, when I look in the mirror, I don't see what the occupational health guy sees, or what my sergeant sees when they tell me I'm looking gaunt. They use words like that—gaunt, frail. I don't see that at all. \n\nWhen I stand in front of that mirror, usually right after the scale, my eyes just zero in on my stomach and my waist. That's the battleground right there. If I can pinch anything, if there's any softness, any lack of definition around the beltline... it's just unacceptable. I'll stand there, turning side to side, checking the lines, checking the firmness. And honestly, I judge my whole day by what I see in those few minutes. If I look lean enough, if my stomach is flat and tight, then I feel like I can respect myself. I feel like I've earned the right to put on the uniform and go out there and do my job. But if I don't... if I see even a hint of slackness, it just ruins me. I feel disgusted. I feel like a fraud. It's like, how can I demand respect on the streets if I can't even maintain discipline over my own body? So, it's not a specific weight, exactly. It's a standard. A standard of looking lean enough that I don't feel ashamed of the man looking back at me.\n\nDoctor: Do you think you would still restrict your food intake if you didn't have concerns about your weight?\n\nPatient: Well, if I didn't have concerns about my weight... see, it's really hard to separate the two. It's all tied up in this whole idea of discipline I was just talking about. They made this whole big deal out of it, acting like I'm some sort of liability to my partner. \n\nThey wanted to know exactly what my daily routine is, and... well, most days, I just keep it to black coffee while I'm on shift. It keeps me sharp, you know? You don't want to be sluggish or weighed down when you're out on the street, especially not at my age. You need to be ready to move. Even if I didn't care about the number on the scale or the softness around my waist, sitting down to a big plate of food just feels like I'm letting my standards slip. It feels like I'm giving in to comfort, like I'm throwing away all that mental toughness I've built up over thirty years on the force. The act of eating a full meal itself, of getting full and heavy, it just feels like complacency. Like I'm dropping my guard. And I've spent my entire career learning never to drop my guard, so... I just can't bring myself to sit down and eat like everyone else does. It's just not who I am anymore.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like your eating habits are related to trying to achieve a certain body shape?\n\nPatient: Well, yeah, it's definitely tied to the shape, like I was saying about the standard. I know I just sort of touched on this, but to be absolutely clear... it is the shape. That's the ultimate goal. The weight on the scale is really just a number that tells me if I'm in danger of ruining the shape, you know?

I just can't.\n\nDoctor: Do you have a specific weight or body shape in mind that you're trying to achieve?\n\nPatient: Well, it's not like I have a specific number written down on a piece of paper, or a picture of some fitness model taped to my bathroom mirror. It's not about trying to look like someone else, or hitting some arbitrary metric that some doctor—no offense—decided was healthy. It's more about what I see when I look at myself. And the thing is, when I look in the mirror, I don't see what the occupational health guy sees, or what my sergeant sees when they tell me I'm looking gaunt. They use words like that—gaunt, frail. I don't see that at all. \n\nWhen I stand in front of that mirror, usually right after the scale, my eyes just zero in on my stomach and my waist. That's the battleground right there. If I can pinch anything, if there's any softness, any lack of definition around the beltline... it's just unacceptable. I'll stand there, turning side to side, checking the lines, checking the firmness. And honestly, I judge my whole day by what I see in those few minutes. If I look lean enough, if my stomach is flat and tight, then I feel like I can respect myself. I feel like I've earned the right to put on the uniform and go out there and do my job. But if I don't... if I see even a hint of slackness, it just ruins me. I feel disgusted. I feel like a fraud. It's like, how can I demand respect on the streets if I can't even maintain discipline over my own body? So, it's not a specific weight, exactly. It's a standard. A standard of looking lean enough that I don't feel ashamed of the man looking back at me.\n\nDoctor: Do you think you would still restrict your food intake if you didn't have concerns about your weight?\n\nPatient: Well, if I didn't have concerns about my weight... see, it's really hard to separate the two. It's all tied up in this whole idea of discipline I was just talking about. I mean, the whole reason I'm even sitting in this chair talking to you right now—what actually brought me in—is because the occupational health department at the precinct got involved. They pulled me in for a routine eval and the doc there started getting on my case, saying I'm not eating enough to sustain a man on active duty. They made this whole big deal out of it, acting like I'm some sort of liability to my partner. \n\nThey wanted to know exactly what my daily routine is, and... well, most days, I just keep it to black coffee while I'm on shift. It keeps me sharp, you know? You don't want to be sluggish or weighed down when you're out on the street, especially not at my age. You need to be ready to move. So it's just the black coffee, and then... maybe, if I really feel like I need something, I'll have a plain yogurt. Then when I finally get home after a twelve-hour shift, I might have a few bites of chicken at night. Just enough protein to keep the engine running, so to speak. \n\nOccupational health thinks that's completely unreasonable, but if I were to sit down and eat a whole, regular, full meal... it just feels wrong. Even if I didn't care about the number on the scale or the softness around my waist, sitting down to a big plate of food just feels like I'm letting my standards slip. It feels like I'm giving in to comfort, like I'm throwing away all that mental toughness I've built up over thirty years on the force. The act of eating a full meal itself, of getting full and heavy, it just feels like complacency. Like I'm dropping my guard. And I've spent my entire career learning never to drop my guard, so... I just can't bring myself to sit down and eat like everyone else does. It's just not who I am anymore.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like your eating habits are related to trying to achieve a certain body shape?\n\nPatient: Well, yeah, it's definitely tied to the shape, like I was saying about the standard. It's all connected. You know, it's funny... well, not funny ha-ha, but you know what I mean. I was at the tailor a couple of weeks ago—well, actually, it wasn't even a tailor, it was just the quartermaster down at the precinct, old Sal. I've known Sal for twenty years. Anyway, I had to go in and get my uniform altered again. The thing was just hanging off me. I mean, literally hanging, like a kid wearing his dad's suit. The shoulders were sagging, the fabric was bunching up under my duty belt. Speaking of the belt, I've had to punch three new holes in the leather just to keep it from sliding down my hips. I used to be right in the middle notch, perfect fit, for years. Decades, even. And now I'm cinching it past the old notches, pulling it as tight as it'll go. \n\nSo I'm standing there, and Sal is pinning the fabric, and he's giving me this look. You know the look. And then I go in for that occupational health eval I mentioned, and the nurse there—she's this young kid, maybe two years out of nursing school—she puts me on the scale, looks at the chart, looks at me, and tells me my weight is \"dangerously low.\" Dangerously low. While she's standing there telling me I'm dangerously underweight and my uniform is practically swallowing me whole? I just pictured myself in the mirror that morning, and I thought about how there was still that tiny bit of give when I pressed my hand against my stomach. I thought, if I just cut out the yogurt entirely, if I just push a little harder, I could finally get that perfectly clean, sharp line. So, yeah, it's about the shape. Even when they tell me I'm too small, all I can see is that I'm not sharp enough yet. It's like I can't even process the words \"dangerously low\" because the shape... the shape just isn't right yet.\n\nDoctor: Do you think you would consider yourself a success as a police officer if you weren't as lean as you are now?\n\nPatient: Well, that’s the million-dollar question, isn't it? Success. You see, being a police officer—especially when you've been on the force as long as I have, over thirty years now—it’s not just a job you clock in and out of. It’s an identity. When I first joined the academy back in the day, they drilled this concept into us called \"command presence.\" You walk into a room, a domestic dispute, a chaotic scene on the street, and people need to know instantly that you are in charge, that you have authority, and that you are completely in control of the situation. \n\nAnd how do you project that control if you don't even have control over your own physical form? So, to answer your question... no. No, I really don't think I could consider myself a success if I weren't as lean as I am now. If I let myself go, even a fraction of an inch, I’d feel like a total failure. \n\nIt goes back to exactly what I was trying to explain to you earlier about my morning routine. When I look in the mirror, I just don't see what everyone else says they see. But I look in that exact same mirror and my eyes just bypass all of that and focus entirely on my stomach and my waist. That is the ultimate measure of a man's discipline. \n\nI literally judge my whole day, my entire sense of worth, by whether I look lean enough right there at the beltline to respect myself. If I wake up and I look in that glass and I see a flat, hard, perfectly lean stomach, then I can put on the badge. I can go out there and be a cop. I have the right to enforce the law because I am enforcing the strictest laws on myself. But if I wasn't this lean? If I was soft? I wouldn't have any self-respect. And if I don't respect myself, the guys on the street sure as hell aren't going to respect me. I've seen guys on the force who let themselves get a gut, who sit in the cruiser eating junk all day, and they're a joke. I swore I would never, ever be that guy. So my success is entirely tied to keeping that edge, keeping that sharpness, no matter what anyone else thinks they see when they look at me.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel your self-worth would be affected by your weight if you were no longer a police officer?\n\nPatient: Well, even if I handed in my badge and my gun tomorrow... say I just retired, packed up, and moved down to Florida like half the guys in my precinct are always talking about doing... honestly, it wouldn't change a single thing. Because it’s exactly like I was just trying to explain to you a second ago about my morning routine. \n\nYou take away the uniform, you take away the cruiser, and I'm still the exact same guy waking up and doing the exact same thing. It's just... it's how I know I'm still holding the line, even if it's just for myself.\n\nDoctor: Do you think you would still feel the need to restrict your food intake if you didn't have the fear of gaining weight?\n\nPatient: That's... well, that's hard to even wrap my head around. I just don't see why they're making such a big deal out of it when I'm still doing my job just fine.\n\nDoctor: Do you think you would be happier if you were thinner?\n\nPatient: Well, happier? I don't know if \"happier\" is the right word. I mean, happiness is subjective, isn't it? For me, it's not really about walking around with a smile on my face because I dropped a pound or two. It's more about... well, it's about satisfaction, I guess. The satisfaction of knowing I have the discipline to achieve a goal. You see, when you're on the force as long as I have been, you see a lot of guys let themselves go. They hit their fifties, they get comfortable behind a desk or even in the cruiser, and suddenly they're huffing and puffing just walking up a flight of stairs. I swore I'd never be that guy. So, if I were thinner—or rather, if I keep pushing myself to stay lean—it just proves to me that I'm still in control. It proves I haven't lost my willpower. I look in the mirror, and if I see any softness, any sign that I'm slipping into that complacent, middle-aged stereotype, it just eats at me. ========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Could I... could I ever consider myself healthy and respectable without the strict habits and... and this physique? 

Doc, I... I honestly don't know how to even conceptualize that. I mean, my brain just hits a brick wall when I try to picture it. It's like asking me if I could still be a cop without the badge, the gun, the uniform, the training... it's just so baked into who I am at this point. 

Because, you know, I keep coming back to this, and I know I sound like a broken record, but it really all comes down to that moment in the bathroom every single morning. When I look in the mirror... I just don't see what everyone else says they see. I don't see the guy my lieutenant pulls aside to ask if he's sick. I don't see the guy the precinct docs are threatening to bench. I don't see that guy. 

I just focus... I hyper-focus, really... on my stomach and my waist. That's the entire world to me in that moment. And I judge the whole day—my entire capacity to be a respectable man, a capable officer, a person of any worth whatsoever—by whether I look lean enough right there. If I were to let go of the eating habits, if I were to just... eat like a "normal" person, whatever that means, and lose that leanness... I would lose the respect. Not just from others, but from myself. And if I can't respect myself when I look in that mirror, how am I supposed to walk out into the world and expect anyone else to respect me? How am I supposed to command a scene, or back up my partner, if I feel like a soft, undisciplined fraud underneath the uniform? So... no. No, I don't think I could. The physique, the leanness... it's the foundation of my self-respect. Without it, the whole house just caves in.
